speakers.name: Salmaan Allibhai
speakers.title: Chief Actuary and head of data and analytics team

exchanges.question: Quantify YoY and QoQ trends in the newly disclosed new business quotes and bind orders and how to think of them relative to submission growth. Follow-up: given the expense advantage, is Kinsale willing to let the accident year loss ratio deteriorate for more near-term growth?
exchanges.answer: Disclosure added at investor request; more granular numbers are more volatile, so don't overthink a 90-day move; across 25 divisions some have plenty of opportunity and others more competition and slower growth. All product lines are managed to a low 20s ROE or greater, with pricing adjusted in both directions; ROE was 24% for the quarter and he would not expect a meaningful deterioration.

exchanges.question: Anything one-off (e.g. favorable non-cat weather) in the better-than-expected accident year loss ratio, and how should it move with mix shift toward casualty? Also why E&S Homeowners declined 22%, and how the 6/1 reinsurance renewal/retentions will be approached given a below-average hurricane forecast and lower reinsurance cost.
exchanges.responderTitle: Chief Actuary and head of data and analytics team
exchanges.answer: Allibhai: nothing out of the ordinary, no one-time adjustments; seasonality means Q1 current accident year loss ratio is typically a little higher than other quarters. Winston: high-value homeowners market seeing increased competition and Kinsale offering lower limits, so average premium is dropping; Personal Insurance division (also a homeowners book) still growing well. Kehoe: retentions and limits reviewed every year and raised many times over 17 years; cannot commit now to how treaties will be placed; 6/1 renewal date.

exchanges.question: How has casualty competitive behavior (MGAs, admitted carriers) changed over six months and where is it more stable? Follow-up: how much of the submission slowdown is demand vs pullback from irrational pricing, and update on broker expansion initiatives.
exchanges.answer: Market is competitive; growth rate by division is a proxy for competitiveness. Winston: a lot of competition from fronts, MGAs and new companies in long-tail lines, specifically construction, over the last four-five months; premises liability strong and meaningful opportunity in anything auto-related. Kehoe: larger accounts more competitive, small to medium accounts are a safe harbor; ex commercial property submissions up 9%, market competitive but reasonably steady; large-account stress depresses growth until those accounts roll off, then normalization; principally wholesale, supportive of experienced broker teams starting new shops.

exchanges.question: Any change in retention, or is the gap between GWP and submissions mostly pricing, exposure and large commercial property mix? Follow-up: are larger competitors using technology to compete more effectively for small business accounts?
exchanges.answer: Winston: new business and renewal hit ratios have been consistent quarter to quarter for a long time, no big change. Kehoe: no; technology has been a core competency for 17 years, the expense ratio is a proxy for Kinsale's tech lead, and lack of legacy software lets it adopt AI and new tech faster; competitors must speak for themselves.

exchanges.question: Has property pricing reset at a lower level or is it still drifting down? Follow-ups: is the expense advantage already fully deployed rather than used to push growth; and how is the equity portfolio performing?
exchanges.answer: No good news on property; easier comps will be in the second half of the year since commercial property volume is disproportionately in the first six months. Expense advantage is one of several (underwriting control, analytics, conservative reserving with a 17-year record of favorable GAAP development); growth is subordinated to profitability; GWP down 0.5% reflects a shift to smaller average premium, and Kinsale expects to keep growing and taking share but never at the expense of profitability. Equity portfolio about 2/3 actively managed, 1/3 passive (principally S&P 500); since late 2022 lagged the S&P but roughly matched its benchmark Vanguard VYM, due to lower tech weighting and value orientation.

exchanges.question: Of commercial property's $65 million Q1 premium ($375 million last year), what portion is the large property business facing competition? Follow-up: with capital chasing lower returns, will Kinsale's low 20s ROE target need to fall to the high teens long-term?
exchanges.answer: No specific breakout, but average premium in that division is somewhere between $30,000-$40,000 per policy, versus probably north of $50,000 a year or two ago, reflecting lost larger accounts or participating higher in the schedule. Winston: the commercial property division is the standalone large shared and layered division; small property is broken out separately. Kehoe: confident in a low 20s ROE given the underwriting model and cost advantage; views it as about 15 percentage points above the risk-free rate (10-year treasury a little below 5%).

exchanges.question: How does Kinsale's submission growth compare with the overall market or its E&S sub-segment?
exchanges.answer: No specific information on the overall market; brokers canvass the market for clients, so he assumes some commonality between Kinsale's stats and competitors' but does not really know.

exchanges.question: Any slowdown or delay in construction activity affecting opportunities? Follow-ups: sequential trend in general casualty growth (about 11-12% vs low 20s last year); and should cash from operations (up 8%) track net written premium?
exchanges.answer: Winston: no delay seen; Kinsale mostly does not write large project-specific policies; some wrap projects out west and in the northeast are being delayed a little. Kehoe: no sequential general casualty stats to provide today; the 10-K has annual GWP by underwriting division with a three-year look back. Petrucelli: trending cash flow with net written premium is a good way to look at it.
